description: We are an independent team of student researchers and programmers from Pakistan participating in the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. We look forward to building a fun, scientifically accurate educational game for future space explorers!
summary:
A responsive web application that allows players to make decisions for four key elements of an outpost; Power, Oxygen, Shields, and Crew Health. Players will utilise an intuitive decision making system to choose their options, a cinematic day change scene and interactive Mission Control log.

The Challenge Space can be quite an abstract concept when teaching about it. We have solved this issue by using authentic data provided by NASA DONKI and WSA-ENLIL to create an immersive game. Real data such as Kp indexes, CME’s and Solar flares (from November 2026) were used alongside easy to understand educational hints.

Why It Is Important By removing the safe option we teach players that every decision has a cost associated with it. This creates an easy to use and engaging way to educate players about the real world aspects of engineering.
details:
This interactive game simulates a 10-day survival scenario where users have to manage the Mars Outpost Alpha by managing 4 key systems: Power , Oxygen , Shields and Crew Health . The user will have to survive 10 days on Mars whilst facing challenging real life Space Weather effects such as Coronal Mass Ejections (CME’s), X-Ray Flares and Dust Storms on Mars. The user has to make decisions using the Select and Confirm system. If any of the systems reach 0% then the mission will fail. However if they survive all 10 days they are awarded the 3 Star Junior Astronaut Certificate and a final Rocket celebration.

Benefits and Impact:

Space learning for younger children can be quite passive using posters or data. Using Mars Outpost Alpha removes any free decisions from the game and teaches the user that everything involves trade-offs. For example, increasing the radiation shields may mean less power for tonight. Having a browser based game means it can be played straight away in the classroom or at home. This makes children think like real NASA mission planners.

Tools and Technologies:

Front End and Functionality: HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, React were used to create a single page responsive application.

Development: Visual Studio Code and Antigravity was used to develop and improve the project.

NASA Data: NASA’s Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI) was used to collect curated data. The WSA-ENLIL model data was also used (7th-14th November 2026). This data has been used to generate the game with real data such as Solar Flare classifications, Kp Index and CME Speed.

Creativity and Team:

We wanted to make sure that the game had the right balance between science and keeping the game engaging for children aged 7-12. To do this we designed a clean Mission Control page alongside dramatic atmospheric cut scenes before each day and animations showing how resources change. We also added simple Did You Know? sections. We only focused on 4 easy to understand systems to track. We also used curated data from NASA within the application to make sure the game ran quickly and reliably, without any issues when being judged.
